extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia editors deciding whether to create, keep, merge, or delete articles about news events
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for judging whether a particular news event merits its own Wikipedia article, including what sources, scope, duration, and effects constitute notability and alternatives if not notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of notability for events
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is presumed to be notable if it receives significant, non-routine, and persistent coverage in multiple reliable sources with national or global scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the page's nutshell summary. Editors should apply the general notability guideline: significant coverage in multiple, independent reliable sources. Remember Wikipedia is not a news service and not every incident that gains news coverage warrants an article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage must be significant and not in passing; in-depth coverage includes analysis and context and is a stronger indication of notability than mere narration of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer books, feature-length magazine articles, and TV news specialty shows (e.g., Time, Newsweek, The Economist, 60 Minutes) as better indicators. Routine reporting that merely narrates events, lacks thematic connection, insight, or critique is often considered routine and weak evidence of notability. Narrative news reports may be primary rather than secondary sources. Avoid relying on pieces whose main purpose is to highlight an older event rather than provide independent coverage of the new event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration or persistence of coverage indicates whether an event has lasting significance; a short burst of coverage does not automatically confer notability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notability need not be ongoing, but editors should not assume future coverage. Events covered only during/just after an incident, without later analysis or discussion, are likely not suitable. If an event is cited as a case study in multiple sources after initial coverage, this suggests lasting significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An event affecting a local area and reported only by local media is generally not notable; national or international coverage is generally required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local coverage does not justify a separate article regardless of the number of local reliable sources. Be aware that regional outlets of a national channel (e.g., a single Fox News regional station) count as local coverage; repeating coverage across outlets of the same network is usually treated as a single instance of national coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple independent sources are required; multiple citations from a single source or derivative reports do not constitute multiple independent sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A series of reports by one newspaper/channel or multiple outlets republishing the same wire story or press release counts as a single source (see Wikipedia:Bombardment). If mainstream outlets report independently and without substantial reliance on each other, they count as multiple sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine coverage (news values vs. encyclopedic value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine news coverage of announcements, sports, tabloid items, pre-scheduled events, and similar items is not sufficient basis for an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of routine items: planned coverage of pre-scheduled events, wedding announcements, obituaries, sports scores, crime logs, press conferences, film premieres. Such items are often better covered within other articles; run-of-the-mill events that do not stand out are probably not notable. Some routine items (e.g., a wedding) may be appropriate within a biographical article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and media bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloid or yellow journalism is usually a poor basis for an article due to lack of fact checking; consider media bias and the quality of fact-checking in sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of infotainment, churnalism, and 'silly season' reporting from 24-hour news cycles. Some editors account for perceived media bias (e.g., Missing white woman syndrome) when assessing notability. Prefer reliable, well-sourced outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasting effects (precedent or catalyst)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are notable if they act as a precedent or catalyst for lasting societal, legislative, or structural change, or have a permanent, sourced effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: murders leading to legislation (Adam Walsh, Matthew Shepard), large natural disasters that cause widespread destruction and long-term effects (Hurricane Katrina, 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake). Minor events with little impact are probably not notable. Lasting effects may be hard to judge shortly after the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking news — caution and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When an event is still being widely covered, exercise caution before creating a standalone article; early coverage may lack perspective and contain errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the {{currentevent}} template to flag changing content. Consider delaying creation until significance is clearer, or start with a section in a related article that can be split out later. Anticipation (creating an article expecting future notability) is often mistaken. Alternatives while a story develops include merging, userfying, or placing content in the Article Incubator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikinews as alternative for breaking coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are encouraged to write about breaking news events in Wikinews rather than creating Wikipedia articles about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content cannot be moved to Wikinews without re-licensing, but similar coverage can be reworked for Wikinews with a soft redirect from Wikipedia. This avoids premature encyclopedia articles on unfolding events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participants / biographies policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone known only for one event should generally not have a standalone article; if the event is notable, write the article about the event and limit biographical information to what is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow WP:BLP1E and WP:BIO1E. Biographical details should be limited to what can be linked to the event and what is reasonably required to explain aspects of the event. Avoid creating biographies of participants who lack independent notability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to deletion (merging, reworking, widening context)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event's notability is in question, consider merging into an existing article, reworking the article to widen context, or otherwise avoiding undue weight or BLP violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merging content into a related article is often preferable. If no suitable merge target exists, rework to broaden context beyond a single event. Take care not to give the event undue weight or violate biographies of living persons policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts — special notability guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a specific notability guideline for criminal acts: if a matter is deemed a likely crime by law enforcement or judicial authority, it falls under this guideline and intense media coverage can confer notability if coverage meets reliable-source standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'criminal act' includes matters where a crime has been established or deemed likely by authorities (e.g., disappearances deemed likely criminal). If deemed notable and a likely crime, an article should remain even if later found not to be a crime, because notability is unaffected. Ensure coverage meets Wikipedia's reliable-sources standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of related Wikipedia policies and shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should consult and apply related Wikipedia policies when judging event notability (e.g., WP:NOT#NEWS, WP:NTEMP, WP:BIO1E, WP:BLP1E, WP:N/CA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These linked policies provide procedural and content-specific guidance (notability, temporary events, biographies, BLP exceptions, notability for companies/organizations). Use shortcuts like WP:DIVERSE, WP:ROUTINE, WP:GEOSCOPE, WP:BREAKING to find specific guidance referenced on this page.
